title: Longreads + Open Thread
author: @ByrneHobart
text:
LongreadsAlex Bronzini-Vender in NYMag on the late Perry Mehrling. (We linked to his hierarchy of money piece a few weeks ago.) There's a strange cyclicality to the study of economics, where sometimes it makes sense to think entirely in terms of the tangible and the real—the ultimate constraint on a welfare state, for example, is not really the numbers in a budget, but the medical care, housing, and other goods and services that have to be produced, and the people who may or may not want to do the producing. On the other hand, the financial system is a set of abstractions for representing these kinds of things in simplified and more usable ways—instead of saying "I'd like to defer consumption right now, but only if you promise me that you'll get me access to a bundle of goods and services worth slightly more at some point in the future," you just buy a certificate of deposit and you don't have to worry about the details. But that means that managing the abstraction layer, and ensuring that both sides of these transactions understand the mapping between legal contracts and economic reality, becomes important. That's something Mehrling did a great job evangelizing, to the point that if you read his older work now, it feels like he's belaboring the obvious. But that's what every great thinker is going for: that they were weird when they started and by the end they've been promoted to cliché.Ed Caesar in The New Yorker on Brazil's First Capital Command, a more organized than average criminal group. This is a good piece on state capacity: the enforcement of rules and contracts is something for which there's generally demand, where the state is the default supplier. But that means that a state that tries to have more breadth than it can manage will end up accidentally outsourcing this to someone else. The gang in question is, as gangs typically are, murderous, but they're less murderous than their rivals because it's bad for business. This establishes a bad equilibrium, because you have one group that's used to interacting with a porous and incomplete bureaucracy, which is necessarily more effective than that bureaucracy in the contexts in which they're directly compared. Well-functioning institutions are never the default, and while they're durable once they're in place, it's hard to establish them.Mark Humphries in Generative History writes about how GPT-6.2 Astra helped to identify the anonymous creator of a series of centuries-old sketches from the early days of the American fur trade. One of the exciting things about applying agentic AI to history is that to make it manageable to humans, people specialize, but sometimes a specialist in A happens to mention some detail that's incidental to A but critical subject B. You can resolve to read every single scrap of information even tangentially related to a question you're trying to answer, which some people do—it's interesting to look at opposition research in the pre-Internet days and to consider just how much time it took to track down weird things people wrote in their college newspaper, person scandals from before they were famous, etc. So, it can be done. But now, it can be done much more easily, and we'll get a more contextual and hyperlinked form of history out of it.Arpit Gupta on analogies between the decline of Rome and the rise of AI: in the later stages of the empire, Rome offloaded defense to nearby tribes, which got the message loud and clear—Rome is rich and doesn't have the capacity to defend itself. But before that, they outsourced a significant share of their cognitive labor to Greeks, slave and free, whom they conquered and then were mostly co-opted by. One of the things the Romans did well was to keep the legal system Latin, while most other intellectual fields were dominated by Greek. And they got a lot out of this symbiotic relationship, including a successor state that was culturally Greek. But the meta cost they ran was that it was hard for the people in charge to be sure they knew what was going on, since they'd outsourced so much knowing to people who weren't fully part of their system.In Asterisk, Thomas Kirk writes about the long history of human's and grain's mutual domestication. The fact that calories per comparable unit of land have been rising, unsteadily for a while but relentlessly within living memory, is one of those crucial background facts for understanding the world, like having an intuition that computers will keep getting smaller and faster and the amount of data they need will correspondingly rise. One thing this piece highlights is that as yields rise, the supply chain gets more complex: select the highest-yielding crops, and you have a monoculture that's more vulnerable to disease; find the optimal fertilizer, and your crop can be so bounteous that plants literally collapse under the weight of all those cheap calories. At every stage, the fixed cost is higher and there's less certainty, but the more food we grow in the aggregate, the more valuable it is to be able to grow 1% more.In this week's Capital Gains, we consider NYC as an illustration of the microeconomics of micro-politeness. New York has a reputation for being a rude city, but even if that's true in net terms, you'll experience more gross politeness per day if you're a pedestrian moving briskly along the sidewalk, because there are so many tiny opportunities for strangers to make your life slightly more convenient while benefiting themselves. Living on expensive land means living with expensive time, and that colors every interaction in high cost-of-living places.A ReadHaus user asks why, if land taxes are especially efficient when the location rather than the structure is responsible for most of the value, do big cities not have more efficient tax systems. One answer is that these places mostly don't rely on property taxes to fund the government. Income taxes are more populist, and while relying on high earners in cyclical industries is fiscally dangerous, it's politically great—it means that in any given year, the biggest winners are going to have substantial windfalls and won't feel too peeved that they're getting taxed highly, whereas many other people in the same cohort are earning less than their average expected annual income and thus getting a comparative subsidy. The high value of agglomeration creates massive economic rents (especially when agglomeration effects aren't being taxed through a land tax!), and that incentivizes rent-seeking behavior. One successful hedge fund portfolio manager can support lots of home health aids; a single Anthropic employee's tax revenue can fund a whole addict-ranching NGO.

BooksVirtuous Bankers: A Day in the Life of the Eighteenth-Century Bank of England: One marketing angle that's gotten more popular lately is the idea of being cozy. Modern Dungeons and Dragons for example, dares to ask: what if a group of adventurers met at some roadside inn, and then stayed at the inn because it's nice and warm and they can have interpersonal adventures every bit as exciting as slaying those kobolds? This book uses a fairly cozy conceit, where instead of outlining the Bank of England's responsibilities, perks, etc., it looks at what a typical day at the bank was like in the late 1700s, from when the porters and maids show up in the morning to tidy, through a busy day of discounting bills and paying dividends and interest, all the way to the evening when guards would patrol the grounds. (They were mostly looking for thieves or intimidating rioters, but they had another function: at the time, firefighting was a private business, tied to insurance, but it would have been effectively impossible to insure so much wealth, so they had no choice but to handle this on their own.)This is a book about a computer. It's a very old computer that has since gotten some upgrades that let it perform far more efficiently, but back in the 18th century, it was an impressive feat of information technology that could handle many kinds of input and output, cache data in sophisticated ways, and overcome some fundamental technological constraints on accuracy through multiple layers of error-checking. A significant part of the job was just to pay off obligations, in the form of dividends, interests, and principal; some of these were settled by waiting until someone showed up and presented evidence of what they were owed, and sometimes they were delivered by hand. This involved a lot of manual verification: if someone claimed to be Lord So-And-So, it was a clerk's job not to accidentally hand a valuable financial instrument to an imposter. A great deal of the bank's business consisted of cross-checking accounts, spotting forgeries, rolling results up to aggregate numbers that were available for public inspection, etc., but the goal was never to get errors down to zero, just to keep them low.And who worked for the bank? At the top, it was controlled by shareholders, but the senior executives didn't have to work very hard, and they often knocked off early compared to the clerks. Clerks got the job through personal recommendations from the governors, which puts those governors in an interesting position as exemplars of two kinds of finance: they did the formal sort, where a financial institution with assets and liabilities changes the composition of those assets from cash to credit obligations, but they were also in the business of lending their reputational capital to promising young workers who'd hopefully make a good impression. This meant that these clerks were some combination of competent and socially connected to a bank governor.These workers, like plenty of others in that era, had valid complaints about their pay; the compensation system had been fixed long ago, and the cost of living in London kept rising. On the other hand, that happened because London was a busy city full of commercial opportunities, and workers could capture those. Some clerks had a side business brokering trades for customers, and a few times the book mentions that they also got gratuities from customers. (Yes! Don't forget to tip your central banker.)The bank at the time served more of an administrative function, rather than enacting policy. But they did have some freedom to affect the money supply. A big part of their business was discounting, or replacing some receivable with an upfront cash payment. They did this on fairly standard terms, but because they had more liquidity than most institutions, and since the governors tended to be connected to the world of commerce, they could also use this to inject liquidity at times of scarcity. So in this book we see the beginnings of monetary policy, in the form of a light conflict of interest.Conservative Parties and the Birth of Democracy: Go back a few hundred years, and the default political arrangement in most of Europe is a system with an extremely narrow class that had any meaningful political representation, by design. Today, they're all pretty democratic. Sometimes, this happened through some kind of complete collapse of the old regime, but in many cases, there was a gradual evolution. This book makes the case that one of the critical institutions for making this transition a healthy one is a party that represents those old elites, and that basically negotiates a gradual devolution of their power. It's history, so we don't have a big sample size, but the book goes pretty deep into the two case studies it cares about, 19th and early 20th century Britain and Germany.The simplest way to think about this is that if there's some party that represents the interests of, say, 5% of the country, then once more than 10% of the people have a vote, that party is permanently out of power. Elites are aware of this, too; even Otto von Bismarck told an interviewer that he expected Germany to follow the path of the UK, though he was careful to say that he had no comments on the likely timing. There are two things the parties can do: broaden their mandate, or limit the extent to which suffrage actually changes who's in charge.The approach the UK's Tories took was to broaden the interest group. They took advantage of the Glide Path Theory of social groups: if they start out high-status, they can continually expand by letting less prestigious people in. This works for social networks, and is part of what makes Bloomberg such a good business. In the UK context, what it meant was that joining a Tory organization like the Primrose League meant hanging out with The Right Sort of People. A hereditary elite would ideally have a rigid class system that limits mobility so they don't have competition, but the next best thing is a slightly looser social hierarchy where people are absolutely thrilled to rub elbows with important people. This naturally broadened the party's constituency: if the party used to represent local landowners, and it tries to coopt local business owners, it's suddenly a bigger party—and now aspiring business owners want to join, too. So as effective suffrage gets expanded from almost no one to effectively everyone, the party always attracts people who would want to preserve the next iteration of the status quo.Germany did it differently. Their aristocracy was a little more fixated on preserving power, not just as a class but in reference to other aristocrats, so they didn't like the idea of forming a big club where they'd all get together and agree on how fast they'd eliminate its exclusivity. In Prussia in particular, election laws gave enormous power to local magnates, who would either bribe voters to vote their way or just strike them from the voting rolls if they didn't. In the short term, the result was that German elections where the median voter favored moderate or left parties, the Junkers could still squeak by with a majority. But it also resulted in Germany having the biggest and best-organized left-wing party; nothing like a sense that the system is rigged to encourage people to consider more revolutionary options. They ended up cycling through a few, and perhaps by the end the Junkers might have felt that a National Liberal)-dominated government that didn't collapse into anarchy or fascism might not have been so bad, all things considered.The result of all of this is that conservative parties end up being a critical element for surviving the transition to democracy, not because they're part of it, but because at every step they're slowing it down to a speed elites can tolerate. From a Whig history perspective, they basically perform the role of public defenders, negotiating down from a weak position but ensuring that nobody can say their opinion didn't matter.Open ThreadDrop in any links or comments of interest to Diff readers.Other than conservative political parties and early central banks, what are some good institutions for The Diff to look at next?Leave a CommentDiff JobsCompanies in the Diff network are actively looking for talent.
